chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ishaq al-Azraq al-Sa'igh said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who dedicated a camel to God, slaughtering it in Kufa as an act of gratitude. He said to me, 'He must slaughter it where he dedicated it to God. And if he did not specify a city, then he must slaughter it opposite the Ka'bah, like the slaughtering of the sacrificial animals (udhiyah). And whoever performs Tamattu' on behalf of his mother and enters the state of Ihram for Hajj on his father's behalf, he has the choice regarding the slaughter; if he does it, it is better, and if he does not, there is no penalty upon him.'

key_terms.أَهَلَّ: He entered the state of Ihram
key_terms.بَدَنَة: A specific type of sacrificial camel or cow dedicated to God
key_terms.تَمَتَّع: To perform Tamattu' (a type of Hajj)
key_terms.مَنْحَر الْبُدْن: The place of slaughtering the sacrificial animals

ai.seo_question: Where should a dedicated sacrificial animal be slaughtered if no specific location was designated?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* clarifies the geographical constraints for fulfilling a vow of sacrifice (*badanah*), emphasizing that the designated location takes precedence unless unspecified, in which case the ritual mirrors the standard Hajj sacrifice opposite the Ka'bah. It further distinguishes the ruling for *Tamattu'* Hajj performed on behalf of others, granting the performer discretion in the slaughter location without penalty for deviation, reflecting the flexibility Shia jurisprudence allows in fulfilling personal vows versus obligatory rites.
